docs.title: StaticSets
docs.text:
Manage sets of static Pods from Kubernetes.

A StaticSet describes a workload that must become a static Pod: a Pod definition persisted on a host and started by that host's kubelet, so that it returns after a reboot even when the Kubernetes API is unreachable. You write a PodTemplateSpec you already know; the operator compiles it into a self-contained Pod, materializes the configuration it references on the node, writes it durably where kubelet looks, and keeps it in step as the template and its configuration change.

The workload itself is never scheduled by Kubernetes, but its placement is: the controller creates a temporary scheduling probe that the cluster's scheduler places and that no node can start, and the node each probe Pod landed on then gets the real static Pod from that node's manager. Two long-lived processes do the work — one cluster-wide controller and one manager per node — and neither of them decides anything the other could get wrong.

docs.title: Development
docs.text:
This project follows the conventions of the repository template it was bootstrapped from. See the contribution guide and the local setup guide.

uv sync                    # install dependencies
uv run pytest tests        # run the test suite
uv run ruff check .        # lint
uv run pyright .           # type-check
uv run vtr build-docs      # build this documentation

The end-to-end suite drives a real cluster and is skipped unless STATIC_SETS_K8S_INTEGRATION=1 is set with kubectl, docker and helm available; the image smoke test needs STATIC_SETS_IMAGE_SMOKE=1 and a Docker daemon. How to check quality lists every gate and what it covers.

docs.title: Placement and capacity
docs.text: A static Pod is never scheduled. kubelet starts the file it finds, on the node whose kubelet finds it — so "where should this run" is a question the cluster's scheduler never gets asked on the workload's behalf. This page describes how the operator asks it anyway, and what that costs.

docs.title: The scheduling probe
docs.text:
For every StaticSet, per generation, the controller creates a scheduling probe: an ordinary ReplicaSet (in Deployment mode) or DaemonSet (in DaemonSet mode) whose Pod template is the workload's scheduling-relevant shape and nothing else:

  • every container is replaced by an inert image, and carries only the workload's resources and its published hostPorts;
  • init containers are mirrored the same way, because their requests affect scheduling;
  • hostNetwork is copied, because two host-network Pods conflict on a port;
  • spec.placement — node selector, node affinity, tolerations, topology spread constraints — is copied onto the probe's Pods;
  • the template's labels are copied, so a spread constraint that selects them matches.

What the probe does not carry is anything that could execute: no command, no arguments, no environment, no volumes, no probes. And it runs under a RuntimeClass whose handler no container runtime implements, so kubelet binds the Pod, asks the CRI for that handler, fails, and never starts a container.

The result is a real scheduling decision attached to a Pod that never runs:

spec.placement + workload resources  ->  probe Pods  ->  scheduler picks nodes
                                                       ->  each node's manager writes
                                                           the static Pod there

The controller deletes the probe as soon as every chosen node has installed its static Pod and kubelet has published the mirror Pod for it. The reservation is then released, and the decision lives on in the placement records.

docs.title: Why not let the manager pick nodes
docs.text:
Because "the first node that happens to run a manager" is not a placement policy. Concentrating placement in the Kubernetes scheduler is the whole point: node selectors, affinity, taints, spread constraints, preemption and capacity accounting are implemented there, by people who have seen more of them than an operator will.

The manager's job is deliberately dull: it is told which node hosts which revision, and it writes, updates or removes that manifest. It never decides.

docs.title: Resource accounting is a deliberate trade-off
docs.text:
The probe declares the workload's requests, not a token reservation. That is what makes the scheduler's answer meaningful: a node is chosen because it can actually fit what will run there.

It does mean the workload is counted twice while the probe exists — once by the probe, once by the static Pod kubelet is already running. The overlap is bounded by one installation: the controller deletes the probe as soon as the static Pod is installed and mirrored. After that, the scheduler does not see the workload's usage at all.

That second half is not a bug in the probe; it is the nature of a static Pod. Nothing outside kubelet accounts for it. The operator's position:

  • capacity is checked at placement time, with the real requests, which is the moment a wrong answer is still recoverable;
  • a static Pod that grows past its declared requests is invisible to the scheduler, exactly like a systemd unit;
  • if placement must respect capacity continuously, express it as policy — pin the StaticSet to a node class with spec.placement.nodeSelector or node affinity.

docs.title: Placement identity is per node
docs.text:
A placement is identified by the owning StaticSet's UID and the node name — never by the manager Pod that happens to serve it:

  • when a manager is replaced, its successor computes the same identity, adopts the same placement directory, record and revisions, and re-acknowledges them. Nothing is orphaned and nothing is duplicated;
  • the static Pod's name carries the revision: <set>-<identity>-<revision>, so two revisions of one placement are two different Pods, which is what makes an overlap expressible at all;
  • a stale manager that comes back to life fails its ownership check and cannot delete its successor's workload.

docs.title: Update strategies
docs.text:
spec.update.strategy decides how a new revision replaces the one a placement carries.

Strategy Behaviour Use when Recreate (default) The old static Pod is removed before the new one is written. Always, unless you have a specific reason not to. At most one revision exists on a node at any moment, and the workload is down for the length of one installation. Surge The new static Pod is written first and the old one is removed once the new one is observed running. You would rather have two revisions briefly than a gap. spec.update.maxSurge bounds how many placements may overlap.

Recreate combined with maxSurge is rejected, because the two contradict each other.

A rollout also re-asks the scheduler: a new generation means a new probe workload, so a placement may move to a different node — that is a relocation, and the operator records it as such. Under Recreate the old probe is deleted before the new one is created, because it holds the capacity the new pass needs; under Surge both exist until the new placement is installed.

If the new revision never comes up under Surge, the previous one is not retired: the placement reports that it is still installed, and the old static Pod keeps running. Two revisions on one node is the price of no gap, and it is reported rather than hidden. A third revision arriving while that is still true retires the oldest, because three revisions on one node is worse than the gap.

docs.title: Availability versus fencing
docs.text:
Fencing — guaranteeing that a node cannot keep running a workload you have retired — takes time, because it depends on that node doing something (removing a file). Any system that claims instant fencing is either lying or has the API server still attached, which is exactly what a static Pod is for.

The operator's choice is to fence conservatively and report honestly:

  • nothing is removed until the node's own manager acknowledges it;
  • a node that cannot be reached keeps its pending cleanup and is reported as such;
  • the only way to stop waiting is an explicit administrative policy (spec.cleanup.onNodeUnreachable: AbandonAfterGrace), which still never claims the remote workload was removed — only that the operator stopped tracking it.

docs.title: What a StaticSet guarantees, and what it does not
docs.text: A static Pod is a Pod that a node owns rather than the cluster: kubelet reads a manifest from a directory on its own filesystem and starts it. Kubernetes finds out about it afterwards, as a mirror Pod it cannot edit and must not schedule. That is the whole point — the workload keeps running, and comes back after a reboot, without the control plane being reachable.

docs.title: The guarantee
docs.text:
After an installation has been acknowledged, kubelet restarts the last installed revision following a host reboot, without Kubernetes API access.

"Restarts" here means kubelet starts the containers again from the manifest it finds. Whether they come up depends on the same things it always does, which is why the next section exists.

docs.title: What that depends on
docs.text:
The guarantee is about the manifest, not about the application. It holds only while these are true on the node:

  • Images are present locally. A container whose image is missing will not start without a registry. spec.offline.imageProvisioning decides whether the operator simply reports that images are externally provisioned, or refuses to publish a revision until they are confirmed present.
  • The container runtime and networking are up. A static Pod uses the node's runtime and CNI like any other Pod; kubelet restoring a manifest does not restore a broken runtime.
  • Storage is available. Anything the workload mounts from the node must still be there. Kubernetes-backed storage (a persistentVolumeClaim) is rejected outright, because attaching a volume needs the API server.
  • The application's own dependencies are reachable. Data stores, peers, secrets it fetches at runtime: none of that is the operator's promise.

docs.title: What it is not
docs.text:
• Not arbitrary Pod compatibility. Only a conservative, validated subset of the Pod API is compiled; see the translation reference for the exact list. A field the operator cannot represent faithfully is rejected, never dropped, because a static Pod that silently lost a field would start, look healthy, and behave differently from the template it came from.
  • Not a replica count. spec.replicas counts placements, not running copies of the workload. A placement that is relocated can briefly leave two nodes' worth of offline workloads in existence, and a Surge rollout deliberately leaves two revisions on one node for a moment; see placement and capacity.
  • Not an exact replica guarantee during a partition. A partitioned node keeps serving whatever it last installed. Nothing the operator can do from the control plane changes that, and pretending otherwise would be the worst outcome.
  • Not a configuration manager. The operator copies configuration content onto the node at install time. A ConfigMap that changes in the cluster becomes a new revision; a ConfigMap that changes and is then never reconciled does not.

docs.title: Why a scheduler probe and a node manager
docs.text:
The alternative — writing manifests from the controller — would require the controller to have a filesystem relationship with every node, which is both a large privilege and a large failure domain. The other alternative — letting a per-node agent pick its own work — would throw away the cluster's scheduler, which is the only thing that knows about capacity, affinity, taints and topology.

So the work is split along that line:

  • the controller decides what should exist and reports what it observes. It mounts nothing from the host and runs unprivileged. To learn where a workload should run, it creates a scheduling probe — a ReplicaSet or DaemonSet whose Pods carry the workload's resources and the StaticSet's placement rules, and which run under a runtime class no node can start. The scheduler places them; nothing executes;
  • a manager runs once per node, as a DaemonSet, and serves every StaticSet whose placement names its node, in every namespace. It writes, updates and removes the manifests on that node and reports what it did, so a replacement adopts the placement its predecessor left behind rather than creating a second one.

The cost is that installation is asynchronous: a StaticSet is not installed until the node's manager says so, which is why the status distinguishes installed state from observed health instead of collapsing both into "ready".

docs.title: Choosing third-party deps
docs.text:
There are many aspects to consider when choosing which third-party packages to rely on. Bad things can happen, if choices are not made wisely, as perfectly illustrated by this XKCD comic:

Arguably the most important aspect is whether packages currently have known vulnerabilities. Accordingly, a whole fleet of tools and platforms exists for scanning your deps to that end, some freely usable. For looking up singular packages online, any one of these is good for use:

  • LFX-Insights: Curated info on popular code projects
  • deps.dev: Exhaustive info on Python and other packages
  • Snyk Advisor: Exhaustive info on Python and other packages

vulnerability = bug or backdoor in the source code, which can be used by an attacker to disturb the software, get unallowed access or steal data

For Python packages specifically, an open-source tool exists for scanning all your dependencies for vulnerabilities at once: pip-audit, which is in fact used within this repo.

Beyond that, package health in terms of maintenance and code quality is another important signal, that ideally serves to prevent vulnerabilities alltogether.

docs.title: Installing dependencies
docs.text:
All dependency installation should be done using uv. See the official docs for details. Tl;dr: uv add PACKAGE_NAME to add it to the core library dependencies, uv add --group GROUP_NAME PACKAGE_NAME to add it to a specific group.

See /pyproject.toml for a list of all dependency groups with descriptions in the comments.

docs.title: How to check quality
docs.text: Certain checks are run by VSCode automatically as you edit code, while others have to be run manually using the VSCode UI, tasks or commands in the terminal.

docs.title: Automatic checks
docs.text:
• Linting via ruff
  • Type-checking via pyright

Discovered issues by these tools will show up as yellow or red squiggly lines underlining your code.

docs.title: Manual checks
docs.text:
Pytest test cases can be run via the VSCode tests UI (beaker symbol in left sidebar) or uv run pytest tests in the terminal.

VSCode tasks can be run via the UI by clicking ctrl + shift + P to open the command palette and then typing Run task, or in the terminal via vtr TASK_NAME. Please run all tasks with the prefixes assert-, build- and info-. Make sure none of them fail and that their printed information does not hint at any major issues.

docs.title: What each gate covers
docs.text:
Command Checks uv run ruff check . Style, imports, naming, docstrings (Google convention), complexity. src/ requires full docstrings; other trees do not. uv run ruff format --check . Formatting, including Python fences inside docs/*.md. Run uv run ruff format . before it, or a file you never edited will fail. uv run pyright . Types across src, app and tests. The operator entry point is a top-level module kopf loads by path, so [tool.pyright] extraPaths tells Pyright where to find it. uv run pytest tests --cov=src --cov=app --cov-fail-under=90 The fast suite plus the coverage bar the contribution guide sets. uv run vtr build-docs The documentation builds. uv run vtr assert-license-compliance Every dependency's licence is acceptable. uv run vtr assert-no-vulnerabilities Known vulnerabilities in the dependency tree. pip-audit reports based-operators as unauditable because it is installed from Git rather than from PyPI. uv run vtr assert-no-deptry-issues No unused or undeclared dependencies, and no direct import of a transitive one. uv run app/render_crds.py Regenerates the CRD in the chart from the models. The same rendering is asserted by tests/app/test_manifests.py, so a forgotten regeneration fails the suite instead of shipping.

Helm is needed by tests/app/test_manifests.py, which renders the chart. That test fails rather than skips when helm is missing while CI is set, so a CI image that loses Helm cannot pass vacuously.

docs.title: Run the suite on Linux before trusting it
docs.text:
Several tests create symbolic links, which Windows refuses without Developer Mode, so they skip on a Windows workstation and run on the Linux CI runner. A change that only breaks on the LINUX branch therefore looks green locally. Reproduce the CI run in a container before pushing:

docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/src" -w /src python:3.13-slim sh -c '
  apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y -qq git
  pip install -q pytest pytest-cov pyyaml
  UV_DYNAMIC_VERSIONING_BYPASS=0.0.0 pip install -q .
  python -m pytest tests -q'

docs.title: Suites that need real infrastructure
docs.text:
They skip by default and are opt-in, because they build images or drive clusters:

Command Needs STATIC_SETS_IMAGE_SMOKE=1 uv run pytest tests/test_image_smoke.py -v A Docker daemon. Builds deploy/Dockerfile and runs both entry points inside the image. STATIC_SETS_K8S_INTEGRATION=1 uv run pytest tests/test_e2e.py -v A reachable cluster, plus docker, helm and (for kind) kind. Installs the chart, creates a StaticSet, waits for the manifest the node manager wrote and for kubelet's mirror Pod, and deletes the StaticSet to exercise the cleanup protocol.

The end-to-end suite points staticPodPath at a directory kubelet does not watch, so it is safe on a kind cluster whose control plane is itself static Pods. What it therefore does not prove is that a rebooted kubelet starts the manifest; that is the manual procedure in How to verify the disconnected reboot guarantee.

docs.title: Types of Contributions
docs.text:
The nature of a contribution roughly aligns with the folders/files, in which it happens, and can be divided into 5 types:

  1. Refactoring contributions may add/modify any files in the repository, but are not allowed to change the public interface of modules in /src or applications in /app, nor make content changes to anything in /docs. This may be ensured by not changing any code in /tests during refactoring, though this is not a requirement.
  2. Documentation contributions only add/modify files in /docs.
  3. Library contributions add/modify modules in /src and may include Documentation contributions related to the changes in /src. Additionally, they must add cases in /tests/src to cover at least 90 % of the contributed code.
  4. Application contributions add/modify notebook scripts (in the form of Jupytext) in /app. These may be rather abstract interfaces for general use of library code, or manifest very specific use cases including elaborate explanations within the notebooks. They may include Library contributions required by respective applications. Additionally, they must add cases in /tests/app to cover at least 90 % of the contributed code.
  5. Major Upgrade contributions include larger, breaking changes to the repository, and as such are not restricted in what they add/modify. However, these contributions will trigger a major version change and thus need to be coordinated carefully with the maintainers.

docs.title: Pull Requests
docs.text:
Any contribution should be made via forking the repo / branching off main and later merging all changes back using a Pull Request (PR) (or Merge Request (MR) on GitLab). Every PR should have a single contribution type (see above), which has to be mentioned at the beginning of the PR title like so:

<Contribution type>: <Rest of your title>

If multiple types apply to your contribution, pick the one with the highest number in the list above.

For the rest of the PR description, please use the PR template.

docs.title: Developing locally
docs.text: Please refer to the local setup guide to get started with working on your local copy of the repo.

docs.title: Commits and Issues
docs.text: Larger contributions / PRs should be split into multiple commits with their own types according to the Gitmoji Spec. If a commit addresses an existing Issue on GitHub / GitLab / etc., please reference that issue via #<ISSUE_ID> somewhere in the commit message. If it resolves the issue (meaning it should be closed), add a footer line to the commit message with Closes:, Fixes:, or Resolves: followed by the issue reference. Make sure you plan ahead how to split up your contribution into commits and in which order.

docs.title: Writing Good Code
docs.text: Please adhere to coding conventions and use tooling as described in this reference. In case you plan on adding any new external (pip) dependencies, please refer to this guide in doing so. Finally, once you are ready to push your code and make a pull request, please make sure you check its quality locally first according to this guide.

docs.title: The Complete Workflow
docs.text:
The entire workflow for making a contribution goes roughly as follows:

  1. Create a fork or banch to work in.
  2. Clone your fork / branch and open it in VSCode.
  3. Install all recommended extensions.
  4. Install/update dependencies via the VSCode task update-dependencies.
  5. Make one or more commits adhering to Gitmoji Spec.
  6. Run local checks and make sure all pass.
  7. Push your commits and make a PR with a title conforming to above spec and description according to the PR template.
  8. Have a kind interaction with the maintainers in the PR comments, get approval, and merge 😊.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A Kubernetes cluster, 1.27 or newer.
  • kubectl and helm.
  • A container image built from this repository (see below).
  • cert-manager only if you want strict admission validation; the default install does not need it.

docs.title: 1. Build and push the image
docs.text:
docker build -f deploy/Dockerfile -t ghcr.io/EXAMPLE/static-sets:0.1.0 .
docker push ghcr.io/EXAMPLE/static-sets:0.1.0

One image carries both processes: the controller that decides what should exist and where, and the node manager that writes the static Pods on each host. Both are derived from the same library, so they cannot disagree about the revision hashing or the ownership protocol.

docs.title: 2. Install the chart
docs.text:
helm install static-sets ./deploy/helm/static-sets \
  --namespace static-sets --create-namespace \
  --set image.repository=ghcr.io/EXAMPLE/static-sets \
  --set image.tag=0.1.0

The controller is cluster-wide: a StaticSet may live in any namespace, and the node that serves a placement is named by the placement rather than by its namespace. The chart therefore installs a Deployment, a DaemonSet (one manager Pod per node), a cluster-scoped RuntimeClass the scheduling probes ask for, and two ClusterRoles — one for each process, neither of which can do the other's job.

The manager mounts two host paths on every node: kubelet's static Pod directory (manager.staticPodPath, default /etc/kubernetes/manifests) and its bundle (manager.bundleDir, default /var/lib/static-sets). Both are values, and a node whose kubelet is configured differently needs them set accordingly:

helm install static-sets ./deploy/helm/static-sets   --namespace static-sets --create-namespace   --set manager.staticPodPath=/var/lib/kubelet/manifests

If your cluster manages RuntimeClass objects centrally, set probe.createRuntimeClass=false and create staticsets-scheduling-probe yourself — it must have a handler no container runtime implements, because a probe Pod that could start would run next to the workload.

docs.title: 3. Decide about the admission webhook
docs.text:
The generated CustomResourceDefinition is a structural schema, so the API server prunes a field it does not know rather than refusing it. With the webhook off (the default), a template field the operator cannot compile is dropped silently before the operator ever sees it.

Turn it on to have such an object rejected instead:

helm upgrade static-sets ./deploy/helm/static-sets --namespace static-sets \
  --set image.repository=ghcr.io/EXAMPLE/static-sets \
  --set image.tag=0.1.0 \
  --set webhook.enabled=true

This needs cert-manager (the chart creates a self-signed Issuer and a Certificate, or point webhook.certManager.issuerRef at your own). The webhook also refuses the policy violations the compiler would otherwise only catch at install time: a privileged workload, a Secret read into the environment.

docs.title: 4. Verify
docs.text:
kubectl -n static-sets rollout status deployment/static-sets
kubectl -n static-sets rollout status daemonset/static-sets-manager
kubectl get crd staticsets.staticsets.cloudlane.dev
kubectl get crd staticpodplacements.staticsets.cloudlane.dev
kubectl get runtimeclass staticsets-scheduling-probe

Then follow How to write a StaticSet.

docs.title: Upgrades
docs.text:
The operator is a Deployment with a single replica and Recreate strategy: two controllers reconciling the same objects collide, so the new one replaces the old one rather than rolling over it. Upgrading the image is therefore:

docker build -f deploy/Dockerfile -t ghcr.io/EXAMPLE/static-sets:0.2.0 .
docker push ghcr.io/EXAMPLE/static-sets:0.2.0
helm upgrade static-sets ./deploy/helm/static-sets --namespace static-sets \
  --set image.repository=ghcr.io/EXAMPLE/static-sets --set image.tag=0.2.0

Manager Pods are replaced by the DaemonSet, and each replacement adopts the placements its predecessor left, so an upgrade does not reinstall the workloads. Only the controller is Recreate: two controllers reconciling the same objects collide.

Schema changes need the CRD applied by hand. Helm installs CRDs from crds/ and never upgrades them:

kubectl apply -f deploy/helm/static-sets/crds/

The CRD in the chart is generated from the models (uv run app/render_crds.py), and the test suite fails if the committed file has drifted from them.

docs.title: Rollback
docs.text: Roll the operator image back with helm rollback, or pin the previous tag. Your workloads are unaffected: they are static Pods on nodes, not objects the controller owns. The older controller version will still understand a CRD that has only gained optional fields, which is the reason to keep schema changes additive.

docs.title: Uninstall
docs.text:
helm uninstall static-sets --namespace static-sets
kubectl delete crd staticsets.staticsets.cloudlane.dev
kubectl delete crd staticpodplacements.staticsets.cloudlane.dev

Deleting the CRD deletes every StaticSet, and each one's finalizer keeps it alive until its placements have acknowledged cleanup. If a node is unreachable the finalizer waits, and kubectl get staticset -o yaml says why. Nothing is force-removed without spec.cleanup.onNodeUnreachable: AbandonAfterGrace; see the installation reference.

Deleting the chart's namespace does not remove the static Pods: they live on nodes. Delete the StaticSets first, or accept that the manifests stay behind and are not tracked by anything.

docs.title: How to setup this code repo locally
docs.text: ⚠️ mind all the inline links. They are helpful :-)

docs.title: 1. System setup
docs.text: A handful of applications need to be installed directly onto your OS. These are all listed in files contained within this repo, which can be directly parsed by a package manager. Exact steps depend on which OS you have:

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
Download the file configuration.winget from the repo's top-level directory, then open your Downloads-folder and double-click the file.

Installation may take a while depending on the speed of your PC and internet connection.

During installation, you may be asked to grant admin privileges multiple times. Please do so. Installers are all official and verified.

docs.title: MacOS or Linux
docs.text:
1. Install Homebrew
  2. Download the file Brewfile from the repo's top-level directory
  3. Open a terminal, cd to your download folder, and run this command:
brew bundle install --file Brewfile

docs.title: 2. Clone Git repo via VSCode
docs.text: See this offical guide.

docs.title: 3. Install all recommended VSCode extensions
docs.text: VSCode should prompt you for exactly that right after cloning the repo. If so, click Yes. If not, go to the extensions tab in the left sidebar, enter @recommended in the search bar and install all manually:

docs.title: 4. Install all Python dependencies via UV
docs.text:
Open an integrated terminal in VSCode (e.g. via shortcut CTRL + Ö) and enter uv sync. This should rather quickly install all required packages, as defined in pyproject.toml.

If you have trouble executing uv in the terminal, try restarting VSCode or installing UV again via the official script.

docs.title: How to verify the disconnected reboot guarantee
docs.text:
The guarantee is that kubelet restarts the last installed revision after a host reboot without Kubernetes API access. That cannot be verified from a controller test: it needs a host that boots, a kubelet that reads a file, and no API server reachable. This page is the reproducible procedure.

What CI verifies (STATIC_SETS_K8S_INTEGRATION=1, see tests/test_e2e.py): on a real cluster, a StaticSet is placed by the scheduler, the node's manager compiles the workload, materializes its configuration, writes the manifest into kubelet's own directory, acknowledges the placement, and kubelet publishes the mirror Pod for what it started — then the whole thing is removed again on cleanup. The suite pins the workload to one node, so it can run against a kind cluster whose control plane is itself tagged with static Pods, without ever touching one of them.

What CI does not verify: that a rebooted kubelet starts that manifest. That is this procedure.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A Linux host with kubelet installed and a container runtime, able to join a cluster and then be disconnected from it.
  • An image the workload uses, already present on that host.
  • kubectl access to the cluster while it is connected.

docs.title: 1. Install with an explicit static Pod path
docs.text:
Use a StaticSet whose staticPodPath matches the host's real kubelet configuration (kubelet --pod-manifest-path, or staticPodPath in the kubelet config file). Do not guess it: the operator never edits kubelet configuration, so a mismatch is a silent no-op at the kubelet level.

# The manager's paths are the node's, so they are chart values, not StaticSet fields.
helm get values static-sets -n static-sets | grep -A3 manager:
# manager:
#   staticPodPath: /etc/kubernetes/manifests   # must match kubelet
#   bundleDir: /var/lib/static-sets

kubectl apply -f reboot-test.yaml

docs.title: 2. Confirm the acknowledged install
docs.text:
kubectl get staticset reboot-test -o jsonpath='{.status.placements[*].revision}{"\n"}'
kubectl get staticset reboot-test -o jsonpath='{.status.placements[*].acknowledged}{"\n"}'

Both must be non-empty and true. An unacknowledged placement means the node's manager never finished, and a reboot test on top of it proves nothing.

docs.title: 3. Record what the node has, without the cluster
docs.text:
On the host:

ls -l /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/reboot-test-*.yaml
ls -l /var/lib/static-sets/placements/*/revisions/*/
cat /var/lib/static-sets/placements/*/ownership.json

Save those outputs. They are the baseline you will compare against after the reboot.

docs.title: 4. Disconnect the node
docs.text:
Stop or block the node's access to the API server, for example:

sudo iptables -I OUTPUT -p tcp --dport 6443 -j REJECT
sudo iptables -I INPUT -p tcp --sport 6443 -j REJECT

Also make sure the mirror Pod's record disappears from the API server's point of view (the node will go NotReady); that is expected and is not a failure.

Do not simply stop kubelet. The guarantee is about a reboot, and a reboot restarts kubelet; stopping it only tests the operator's offline behaviour, which is a different (also covered) claim.

docs.title: 5. Reboot the host
docs.text: sudo systemctl reboot

docs.title: 6. Verify, still disconnected
docs.text:
Back on the host, before restoring the network:

# The manifest kubelet reads must be unchanged.
diff <(cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/reboot-test-*.yaml) <your saved copy>

# kubelet must have started it, with no API server involved.
sudo crictl pods | grep reboot-test
sudo crictl ps | grep reboot-test
journalctl -u kubelet --since "10 min ago" | grep -i static

Expected: the manifest is byte-identical, the containers are running, and the workload's own logs show it came up. If the containers are running but the app is not healthy, check the image is present locally and the app's dependencies are reachable — that part is outside the guarantee, as described here.

docs.title: 7. Restore the connection
docs.text:
sudo iptables -D OUTPUT -p tcp --dport 6443 -j REJECT
sudo iptables -D INPUT -p tcp --sport 6443 -j REJECT

Give the node a minute to go Ready, then check that the operator reconnected and did not change anything:

kubectl get staticset reboot-test -o yaml | grep -A3 placements

desiredRevision must equal the revision recorded in step 2. If it changed, the operator computed a different revision offline than it had online, which is a bug: revisions are a pure function of the template and the resolved configuration.

docs.title: 8. Clean up
docs.text: kubectl delete -f reboot-test.yaml

docs.title: Also worth testing while you are here
docs.text:
• Reinstall after a reboot. Delete the StaticSet while connected, reboot, and confirm the manifest is gone and nothing starts. This is the cleanup protocol, not the reboot guarantee.
  • Disconnected revision retention. While disconnected, the last committed revision must stay active. spec.offline.retainedRevisions keeps older revisions on the node so a failed update can be rolled back; the manager never prunes the active one.
  • Image absence. With spec.offline.imageProvisioning: VerifiedBeforeInstall, a revision whose images are not confirmed present is refused, so you cannot install something that will fail after the reboot.

docs.title: Reporting what you observed
docs.text: If you run this, record the kubelet version, the container runtime, the image reference, the revision before and after, and the exact commands. Whether a reboot guarantee holds is a property of a specific node configuration; a version without that context is not evidence.

docs.title: How to write a StaticSet
docs.text: A StaticSet is a PodTemplateSpec plus the placement, update and offline policies a static Pod cannot inherit from anywhere. This guide writes one from scratch; the reference lists every field.

docs.title: 1. Write the configuration it needs
docs.text:
The operator resolves ConfigMaps and Secrets itself, so they have to exist in the same namespace as the StaticSet before it is installed:

apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: web-conf
  namespace: static-sets
data:
  app.conf: |
    greeting=hello

kubectl apply -f deploy/samples/configmap.yaml

docs.title: 2. Write the StaticSet
docs.text:
apiVersion: staticsets.cloudlane.dev/v1
kind: StaticSet
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: static-sets
spec:
  mode: Deployment
  replicas: 2

  placement:
    nodeSelector:
      kubernetes.io/os: linux

  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: web
          image: registry.example.com/web:1.27
          imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
          env:
            - name: GREETING
              valueFrom:
                configMapKeyRef:
                  name: web-conf
                  key: app.conf
          volumeMounts:
            - name: conf
              mountPath: /etc/web
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz
              port: 8080
      volumes:
        - name: conf
          configMap:
            name: web-conf

kubectl apply -f web-staticset.yaml

Worth noting about each part:

  • mode and replicas are a pair. Deployment mode requires replicas: it is how many placements the operator asks the scheduler for, and therefore how many nodes will host the workload. DaemonSet mode must not set replicas, because the DaemonSet controller decides how many placements a pass produces.
  • placement is what the scheduler uses to place the scheduling probe, and therefore the workload. It is not copied onto the workload itself; see placement and capacity.
  • template is an ordinary PodTemplateSpec, restricted to the subset the operator can compile, and it must not carry its own placement fields. Its containers' resources are what the scheduler sees when it decides where the workload goes.
  • Where the manifest is written is not part of a StaticSet: the node manager is configured once per node by the chart (manager.staticPodPath, manager.bundleDir), so a StaticSet cannot widen the host access of the process that writes it.

docs.title: 3. Watch it install
docs.text:
Installation is asynchronous, and happens in visible steps: the controller creates a scheduling probe, the scheduler places it, and the manager on each chosen node compiles the workload and writes the manifest before anything is installed.

kubectl -n static-sets get staticset web -o yaml
kubectl -n static-sets get staticpodplacements -l staticsets.cloudlane.dev/set=web -o wide
kubectl -n static-sets get replicasets -l app.kubernetes.io/component=scheduling-probe

The probe workload is transient: it exists only while the scheduler's answer is being installed, and its Pods never start. The placement records are the durable part.

The status separates what was installed from what was observed:

status:
  observedGeneration: 1
  desiredRevision: r-8a5c...
  placements:
    - identity: e6383089b2
      node: worker-1
      revision: r-8a5c...
      phase: Installed
      acknowledged: true
  health:
    - identity: e6383089b2
      node: worker-1
      observed: true
      phase: Running
      ready: true
  conditions:
    - type: Ready
      status: "True"
      reason: AllPlacementsInstalled

placements is what the node's manager did; health is what kubelet was seen to run. A placement can be Installed and unhealthy, or Installed and unobservable because its node is gone, and the two are never conflated.

docs.title: 4. Change it
docs.text:
Editing the configuration a template references produces a new revision, because the revision is a hash of the compiled Pod and every file it needs:

kubectl -n static-sets patch configmap web-conf \
  --type merge -p '{"data":{"app.conf":"greeting=goodbye\n"}}'

Watch desiredRevision change and the placement re-acknowledge. Editing spec.template does the same. Nothing is removed until the new revision is in place, and the previous revision's files stay for spec.offline.retainedRevisions generations so a rollback has something to roll back to.

docs.title: 5. Delete it
docs.text:
kubectl -n static-sets delete staticset web

The object stays until every placement has acknowledged that its manifest is gone. If a node is unreachable it waits, and the reason appears in the object's status. See the installation reference for the protocol and for the administrative escape hatch.

docs.title: Common refusals
docs.text:
The operator refuses rather than silently dropping. The ones you are most likely to meet, and what to do instead:

Refusal Use instead spec.template.spec.nodeSelector / affinity / tolerations spec.placement serviceAccountName, automountServiceAccountToken Nothing: a static Pod cannot hold an API token offline. imagePullSecrets Pre-pull the image on the node and use imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent. persistentVolumeClaim, any other API-backed volume An emptyDir, or a ConfigMap or Secret volume. hostPath volume in the template Nothing: the only hostPath mounts are the revision directories the operator materializes. volumeMounts[].subPath Separate volumes, or an items mapping that puts the file where you want it. securityContext.privileged spec.policy.allowPrivileged: true, if you accept that nothing reviews the manifest. env[].valueFrom.secretKeyRef A Secret volume, or spec.policy.allowInlineSecretEnv: true if you accept the disclosure.

Every refusal names the field and, where one exists, the alternative. The translation reference has the complete list.

docs.title: Code Checklist
docs.text:
• Code follows the project's conventions for style and tooling
  • Local checks were run and passed (see guide)
  • Any added external dependencies were manually examined for vulnerabilities and maintenance health (see guide)
  • Documentation was updated, if needed
  • PR branch was rebased onto current version of main, if parallel changes occured

docs.title: Command-line interface
docs.text:
The static-set-manager command runs the node manager without kopf. The DaemonSet runs kopf run app/static_pod_manager.py, which is watch-driven; this command does the same work in one pass (or on an interval), which is what an operator wants when debugging a single host: it needs a kubeconfig, not a running controller.

It reads the node and the two host paths from its environment, reads every StaticPodPlacement that names that node, and compiles, installs, retires or removes the static Pods it finds — then reports the outcome in each record's status. Both entry points call the same library functions, so a manual pass cannot behave differently from the DaemonSet.

How that fits into a deployment is described in Installation. This page is the command reference itself, generated from the Typer application's own declaration, so it always agrees with what the command actually accepts:

docs.title: static-set-manager
docs.text: Write this node's static Pods from the placement records that name it.

reconcile repeats its pass every --interval seconds by default, so a configuration change, a moved revision or a cleanup request published just after the previous pass is noticed without waiting for anything; --interval 0 runs one pass and exits.

docs.title: Coding Conventions and Tooling
docs.text:
• VSCode or any derived editor (supporting the VSCode extension system) should be used for code editing.
  • Required VSCode extensions are recommmended in /.vscode/extensions.json and should be installed before starting work on the repo.
  • Core code tooling is directly integrated into VSCode UI (via extensions).
  • ruff is used for linting.
  • black is used for formatting on file save.
  • pyright is used for type-checking (via PyLance).
  • pytest is used for testing.
  • Additional tooling is integrated via VSCode task definitions in /.vscode/tasks.json.
  • They can be executed via vtr TASK_NAME in the terminal as well (provided by vscode-task-runner package).
  • Tasks are divided into different types:
    • assert: Succeed / fail depending on some quality condition (and print additional info to stdout).
    • build: Generate files for various purposes (e.g. docs, package builds, etc).
    • print: Only print info to stdout to be interpreted by a human or LLM.
    • serve: Run some kind of development server (usually with live updates).
  • See task definitions for details.
  • All Python-specific config can be found in pyproject.toml
  • Modern typehints should be used throughout the code and all functions, methods and classes should have Google-style docstrings
  • properdocs is used for docs generation
  • config in /docs/.config.yml
  • mkdosctring.python for API docs
  • mkdocs-typer2 renders the command reference from the Typer applications, so a page never hand-copies an option list
  • properdocs = maintained mkdocs successor
  • Command-line entry points are Typer applications. The command declaration is the single source of truth for parsing, --help and the generated reference page.
  • Kubernetes API access goes through the official kubernetes client, whose generated models are pydantic models. Built-in objects are read and written as those models, and the scheduler-placement types in spec.placement are the generated models themselves; the operator's own models describe only the StaticSet API, because a static Pod template is deliberately narrower and stricter than V1Pod.
  • CI pipelines for both GitHub (/.github/workflows) and GitLab (/.gitlab-ci.yml) exist
  • Checks are run on every push to main or every pull request event, involving most of aforementioned tooling
  • Semantic-release is run on every push to main, leveraging Gitmoji semantics to determine version numbers

docs.title: Deferred features and known limitations
docs.text: This is a working prototype, not a finished operator. This page lists what is not implemented, so that nothing has to be discovered by reading the source.

docs.title: Not verified by automation
docs.text: Item Status Reboot recovery Not verified in CI. The end-to-end suite proves the operator compiles the workload, materializes its configuration, writes the manifest to the configured directory, acknowledges it, and removes it again on cleanup, against a real cluster. Whether a rebooted kubelet then starts that manifest is verified by the manual procedure in How to verify the disconnected reboot guarantee. No automated test in this repository has observed a host reboot. Air-gapped image preparation spec.offline.imageProvisioning: VerifiedBeforeInstall refuses to publish a revision until a checker confirms the images are present, but no checker is shipped: reconcile(..., image_checker=...) is a seam, and the manager supplies none. The default policy (ExternallyProvisioned) reports that image availability is somebody else's responsibility. Real registry / disconnected registry behaviour Not exercised. Pull policies are validated (Always is refused unless the policy accepts it) but no test pulls from a registry or fails to.

docs.title: Accepted but not acted on
docs.text: Field Status spec.update.gracePeriodSeconds Validated, carried, and not used to bound retirement. A placement is retired when its node's manager removes the manifest, not when a timer expires.

docs.title: Deliberately not supported
docs.text:
These are design decisions with reasons, not gaps; they are listed here so the trade-off is visible rather than surprising. Each is also in the translation reference.

  • Secret to environment, offline. Refused unless spec.policy.allowInlineSecretEnv is set. The only offline ways to satisfy the request both disclose the value — write it into the manifest, where the mirror Pod exposes it, or lose it after the reboot — so the operator refuses and offers the Secret-as-a-volume shape instead.
  • Pod affinity and anti-affinity. They describe co-location with other Pods, which a static Pod cannot honour, because kubelet does not run the scheduler for it.
  • hostPath volumes from the template. The only hostPath mounts in an emitted manifest are the revision directories the operator materialized.
  • Any API-backed volume. PVCs, projected volumes, downward API, NFS: all need a source that will not exist offline.
  • Service accounts and image pull secrets. Both are fetched from the API server.
  • A wide slice of the Pod API that has no representation here: lifecycle, terminationMessagePath/Policy, hostAliases sub-cases, topologySpreadConstraints in the workload, priority, overhead, readinessGates, resourceClaims, and anything else the models do not name. They are refused, not pruned — unless the admission webhook is disabled, in which case the API server prunes them first; see the translation reference.

docs.title: Known sharp edges
docs.text: Item Consequence The manager runs as root. kubelet's manifest directory is root-owned, so writing there needs it. Pod Security Admission in a restricted namespace will refuse the manager Pod; install the chart into a namespace with a policy that permits it, or use a node-local kubelet configuration that lets a different user write the path. Static Pods bypass admission entirely. A manifest file is not an API object. spec.policy.allowPrivileged and the webhook are the only guards this operator offers; nothing else in the cluster will see the workload. Capacity is checked once, at placement time. The scheduling probe declares the workload's requests, so the node the scheduler picks can fit it — but once the probe is deleted, the running static Pod is invisible to the scheduler. A workload that outgrows its declared requests is neither rescheduled nor evicted. See capacity. Fencing is eventually consistent. A node keeps running its workload until its own manager removes the manifest. An unreachable node keeps it indefinitely unless AbandonAfterGrace is set, and even then the operator only stops tracking it. One manager per node, one account for the cluster. The manager reads every StaticSet and every ConfigMap and Secret those StaticSets reference, in every namespace. Narrowing that would mean one DaemonSet per namespace, each mounting the same host paths but seeing only its own namespace's placements. Placement is one pass per generation. A new node does not receive a DaemonSet-mode placement until the operator notices it is eligible, and a placement is not moved because a better node appeared: the scheduler is asked again on the next generation, not continuously. A probe pass holds a real reservation for the workload, so running it constantly would cost more than it bought. Drift is repaired on an interval, not immediately. The manager rewrites a manifest that no longer matches the revision it rendered, and it runs a periodic pass per placement (30 seconds by default), so a manifest edited on the node is corrected on the next pass rather than the instant it changes. There is no watch on ConfigMaps or Secrets, and no alert: the repair is visible only as the file changing back. The probe's runtime class is a cluster prerequisite. The probe needs a RuntimeClass whose handler no CRI implements; the chart installs one, and a cluster that manages runtime classes itself must set probe.createRuntimeClass=false and provide it. A placement on a lost node outlives it. Its record is reported as blocked, not deleted: the operator stops tracking it only under AbandonAfterGrace. Deleting the record by hand is safe — its finalizer belongs to a manager that is not there — but the residual manifest on that host becomes untracked.

docs.title: Suggested next steps
docs.text:
In rough order of value:

  1. A dedicated acknowledgment resource (or a lease) instead of a ConfigMap, so a placement's state has a schema and a lifecycle of its own.
  2. A real image checker for VerifiedBeforeInstall, driven by the container runtime's own inventory.
  3. Honour gracePeriodSeconds so a retired placement has a bounded window to confirm termination before it is reported as blocked.
  4. Automated reboot verification, most plausibly a small VM-based job that boots a node image with the manifest already on it and asserts that the containers came up with no API server listening.
  5. Cleanup of orphaned placement records once a StaticSet's UID is known to be gone.

docs.title: Directory Structure
docs.text:
Names of directories and config files in this repository are based on common conventions and requirements of specific development tools, with a few custom ideas on top. Where a directory holds project-specific content, it is described below.

  • .venv: Python virtual environment (not checked out in Git)
  • app: Executable scripts built on the library in src
  • static_sets_operator.py: the controller entry point. This is the file kopf run executes inside the operator image, and the file the based-operators scaffolder loads to derive the CRD and the chart.
  • static_pod_manager.py: the node manager entry point. kopf run executes it inside the manager DaemonSet, one Pod per node; it watches placement records and writes the static Pods on the node it runs on.
  • static_sets_manager/: the static-set-manager command, which runs the same library once (or repeatedly) for one node without kopf — what an operator reaches for when debugging a single host. Also ships as a console script.
  • render_crds.py: regenerates both CRDs in the chart from the Pydantic models, so the committed schemas cannot drift from the types the operator reconciles.
  • deploy: What a cluster needs to run the operator
  • Dockerfile: the operator image, carrying both the controller and the manager.
  • helm/static-sets/: the chart, including crds/ (the generated CRD), the RBAC for both identities, and the optional admission webhook.
  • samples/: StaticSets that the test suite validates, so they always describe objects the operator accepts.
  • docs: Source files (mostly Markdown) for project documentation, named after the Diátaxis mode they are written in: how-to-*.md for tasks, ref-*.md for reference, about-*.md for explanation.
  • src: Source code for the core library modules
  • static_sets/models.py: the StaticSet resource — spec, status and policies.
  • static_sets/workload.py: the supported PodTemplateSpec subset.
  • static_sets/translation.py: the compiler, and what it refuses.
  • static_sets/revision.py: deterministic revision identity.
  • static_sets/install.py: durable installation, ownership and cleanup on a node.
  • static_sets/placements.py: the StaticPodPlacement record — one node's static Pod for one StaticSet.
  • static_sets/probe.py: the scheduling probe, which is how the Kubernetes scheduler is asked for a placement.
  • static_sets/controller.py: the pure reconcile planner and status builder.
  • static_sets/manager.py: the on-node runtime, including the rollout order.
  • static_sets/cluster.py: the cluster-backed implementation of the manager's API.
  • static_sets/paths.py: path validation and durable write primitives.
  • static_sets/api.py: the official Kubernetes client, configured for the operator, with failures classified as "refused" or "unreachable" and absence handled at the call sites that probe.
  • static_sets/validation.py: strict admission validation.
  • static_sets/naming.py: deterministic names, labels and identities.
  • tests: Code for automated testing of library modules and applications (via pytest)
  • tests/src/: unit tests for the library, one module per unit of behaviour.
  • tests/app/: tests for the entry points, the manager command and the shipped manifests (including chart rendering and CRD drift).
  • tests/test_e2e.py: the end-to-end suite against a real cluster, opt-in.
  • .dockerignore: Files excluded from the image build context
  • .gitignore: Files to ignore when committing into the Git repository
  • AGENTS.md: Short map for AI agents, pointing into docs/
  • Brewfile: System dependencies for development on MacOS or Linux
  • configuration.winget: System dependencies for development on Windows
  • pyproject.toml: Central Python project config (dependencies, linting, test config)
  • README.md: Main description of the repository
  • uv.lock: Exact dependency versions determined by UV (generated file)

docs.title: Installation: what ends up on a node
docs.text:
Everything the node manager writes lives beneath two directories it was told about at start-up: kubelet's static Pod path and the persistent bundle directory. This page documents the layout, the two records that describe it, the ownership protocol that protects it, and the cleanup protocol that removes it.

The manager is configured by the chart, once per node — manager.staticPodPath and manager.bundleDir. A StaticSet does not declare either: a StaticSet cannot widen the host access of the process that writes it.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
/etc/kubernetes/manifests/                  kubelet watches this
  web-e6383089b2-r-8a5ca1….yaml             one manifest per placement and revision

/var/lib/static-sets/                       the bundle the manager owns
  placements/
    e6383089b2/                             one directory per placement identity
      ownership.json                        who owns it, which revision, which generation
      cleanup-intent.json                   present only while a cleanup is outstanding
      revisions/
        r-8a5ca1…/                           immutable, revision-named
          manifest.yaml                     the exact manifest this revision rendered
          config/<volume>/…                 materialized ConfigMap files
          secrets/<volume>/…                materialized Secret files, 0400 by default

Two invariants hold throughout:

  • the manifest file name equals the static Pod's name. kubelet derives a static Pod's name from the file it read, so keeping the two identical is the convention every release accepts. The name carries the revision, which is what lets a Surge rollout leave the previous revision's file in place until its successor runs;
  • temporary files, backups and configuration live outside kubelet's watched directory. Writing a partially written file there would make kubelet try to start it.

docs.title: The placement record
docs.text:
StaticPodPlacement is a namespaced custom resource, one per node and StaticSet, named <StaticSet>-<identity> in the StaticSet's namespace and owned by it.

apiVersion: staticsets.cloudlane.dev/v1
kind: StaticPodPlacement
metadata:
  name: web-e6383089b2
  namespace: static-pods
spec:                       # the controller decides this
  staticSet: web
  staticSetUid: 0f9a4b6c-…
  node: worker-1
  generation: 3
  desired: true
status:                     # the node's manager reports this
  identity: e6383089b2
  revision: r-8a5ca1…
  staticPodName: web-e6383089b2-r-8a5ca1…
  phase: Installed
  acknowledged: true
  observedGeneration: 3
  message: installed r-8a5ca1… (updated)

The split matters:

  • the controller writes the spec: which node the scheduler chose, for which generation, and whether the placement is still wanted. Those are the things only the control plane knows;
  • the node's manager writes the status: which revision is installed, whether the write is durable, and why it failed. A per-node manager writing into a shared status would fight the controller for the same field; one object per manager is what an optimistic-concurrency write is designed for;
  • spec.desired: false is the cleanup intent. There is no separate message: the record stays until the manager reports the static Pod gone, and only then does the controller delete it.

Placement records are also why a StaticSet's status can be honest about where its workloads are: the operator's view of a placement is a record the node itself filled in, not an inference from a Pod name.

docs.title: Placement identity
docs.text:
identity = sha256(resource_uid + "\0" + node)[:10]

The identity is derived from the owning StaticSet's UID and the node, never from the manager Pod. Consequences:

  • a replacement manager computes the same identity, so it adopts the same revision directory, the same manifest and the same record instead of orphaning them;
  • two managers can never converge on one placement with different content, because only one of them runs on that node;
  • the static Pod's name is <StaticSet name>-<identity>-<revision>, so names and paths cannot collide between placements, and a placement can never collide with its own successor.

docs.title: The ownership record
docs.text:
placements/<identity>/ownership.json is the authority for every destructive operation:

{
  "placement": "e6383089b2",
  "pod_name": "web-e6383089b2-r-8a5ca1…",
  "static_set": "web",
  "static_set_uid": "0f9a4b6c-…",
  "namespace": "static-pods",
  "node": "worker-1",
  "generation": 3,
  "revision": "r-8a5ca1…",
  "retiring": "r-cf722c…",
  "history": ["r-8a5ca1…", "r-cf722c…"],
  "state": "Installed",
  "owner": "manager-worker-1-6d9f…",
  "updated_at": "2026-10-12T10:00:00+00:00"
}
  • it is written before anything else, so files left by an interrupted installation are still discoverable and attributable;
  • owner is the manager Pod's name, the instance identity. A manager that was replaced finds a different owner and refuses to act, which is what stops it deleting its successor's workload;
  • history is the ordering of revisions. Revision tokens are content hashes, so their names carry no ordering; the record is the only authority for which revision is newer, and retention prunes against it;
  • retiring names the revision whose manifest is still installed while a newer one proves it can run. It is set only between a Surge installation and the retirement that follows it, and it is cleared as soon as the file is removed;
  • generation guards handover: a successor may adopt a placement recorded for an older or equal generation, but a record from a newer generation is authoritative and is never overwritten, so a resurrected older manager cannot reclaim a placement that has moved on.

docs.title: The manager keeps reconciling
docs.text:
The manager is a kopf application. It is told when a placement changes — that is what the watch on StaticPodPlacement is for — and it also runs a periodic pass per placement, because the other half of the desired state is a ConfigMap or a Secret it does not watch. One pass installs and acknowledges; the next ones notice configuration that changed, a revision that moved, and a cleanup that was requested after the previous pass.

The pass never removes anything the API has not asked it to. If the API becomes unreachable it reports that it is offline, changes nothing, and keeps the last committed revision running until the API returns — never treating an unreachable API as an empty desired state.

docs.title: Installing a revision
docs.text:
The order is chosen so that an interruption at any point leaves something consistent:

  1. the placement directory is created with mode 0700;
  2. the ownership record is persisted;
  3. the revision's configuration files are written into an immutable, revision-named directory, each with its declared mode, and each flushed with fsync;
  4. the rendered manifest is written into the revision directory as well, so the exact content that produced the revision survives independently of kubelet's directory;
  5. under Recreate, the previous revision's manifest is removed first; under Surge, the new manifest is written while the old one is still in place;
  6. the new manifest is written to a temporary file next to kubelet's path, fsync-ed, and renamed onto its final name — kubelet sees either the old revision or the new one, never a half-written file;
  7. the record is updated to name the active revision, and the previous one as retiring under Surge;
  8. under Surge, once kubelet reports the new static Pod running, the retiring revision's manifest is removed and retiring is cleared;
  9. obsolete revisions are pruned against history, keeping spec.offline.retainedRevisions of them, and never the active one.

An error anywhere before step 6 leaves the previously active revision intact, which is the "invalid updates must leave the active revision intact" rule.

docs.title: Path and permission safety
docs.text:
• every path the manager builds is validated as being inside the directory it was given: absolute paths, .. segments and escaping item paths are refused;
  • symbolic links are refused at every component on the way to a file it is about to write, and inside any tree it is about to remove;
  • files are created with an explicit mode, never the process umask; the bundle is 0700, records are 0600, Secret files are 0400 by default;
  • the manager only removes directories strictly inside the placement directory it owns. It never removes a bundle root.

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
A finalizer is bookkeeping, not cleanup: it holds the object while the work is done, and it never performs it. Manager termination does not remove a static Pod either — the workload is meant to outlive the process that installed it.

When a placement is no longer wanted — scale-down, deselection, relocation, or deletion of the StaticSet — the controller:

  1. sets spec.desired: false on the placement record, with a reason. The controller has no host access, so the intent travels through the API;
  2. waits for the node's manager, which writes the intent durably to cleanup-intent.json before acting, removes the manifest durably (unlink plus a directory fsync), and only deletes the revision directories once the static Pod is confirmed stopped and removeConfigurationAfterAck allows it;
  3. reports the phase as Cleaning until then, and only Cleaned once the manager says the Pod is gone;
  4. deletes the record and releases the StaticSet's finalizer only after that.

There is no cleanup worker Pod any more: the manager already runs on every node, so the node that has to do the work is the node whose manager is doing it.

The whole protocol is idempotent: removing an already-absent manifest is not an error, the intent is simply re-persisted, and a placement with no local record at all acknowledges immediately.

docs.title: When a node cannot be reached
docs.text:
A placement on a node that does not report Ready has no manager to do the work, so it is reported as Blocked, not chased. The intent stays pending, the message says so, and spec.cleanup.onNodeUnreachable decides what happens next:

  • Retain (default) keeps waiting and keeps reporting. The StaticSet is not released;
  • AbandonAfterGrace lets an administrator stop waiting after abandonmentGraceSeconds. The record is then marked abandoned, the operator stops tracking it, and it never claims the remote workload was removed — a residual static Pod may still be started by that node's kubelet. Removing it is a manual operation on that node.

docs.title: Security notes
docs.text:
Host access. The manager Pod mounts exactly two host paths, both read-write: kubelet's static Pod directory, and the bundle. It runs as root because kubelet's manifest directory is root-owned. It has all capabilities dropped, no privilege escalation, a read-only root filesystem, no host networking or PID namespace, and no other mount. Restricting further would mean either a different kubelet configuration or accepting that installation cannot happen.

One manager, every namespace. The manager serves StaticSets from any namespace, because a placement names a node rather than a namespace. It holds one ServiceAccount for the whole cluster, and that account may read StaticSets and the configuration they reference, read the Pods it needs to observe, and write the status of the placements that name its node. It cannot create a placement, cannot move one, and cannot delete one: where a workload goes is not its decision.

A static Pod bypasses admission. A manifest file is not an API object: no admission controller, no Pod Security Admission, no policy engine sees it. That is why spec.policy.allowPrivileged defaults to refusing a privileged workload, and why the hostPath volume source is refused in templates: those are exactly the cases where normal Pod admission would have been the only guard.

The probe is inert by construction. It names a RuntimeClass whose handler no container runtime implements, and it carries none of the workload's command, arguments, environment or volumes. Even if a node were misconfigured into starting a probe Pod, it would run a pause image and nothing else.

Secrets at rest. Secret material is written to the node's filesystem in plaintext, mode 0400 under 0700 directories, and mounted read-only into the workload. It is never written into the manifest, into status, or into logs. Anyone who can read the bundle directory as root can read it; node encryption, and the choice of bundleDir on a suitably protected filesystem, remain the operator's responsibility.

docs.title: static_sets
docs.text:
Manage sets of static Pods from Kubernetes.

A :class:~static_sets.models.StaticSet describes a workload that must become a static Pod: a Pod definition persisted on a host and started by that host's kubelet, so that it returns after a reboot even when the Kubernetes API is unreachable.

Two processes realise it:

  • the central controller (app/static_sets_operator.py) watches StaticSets in every namespace. To learn where a workload should run it creates a scheduling probe — a ReplicaSet or a DaemonSet whose Pods the real scheduler places and whose runtime class no node can start — and records the scheduler's answer as one :class:~static_sets.placements.StaticPodPlacement per node;
  • the node manager (app/static_pod_manager.py) runs once per node as a DaemonSet, watches those placement records, and writes, updates and removes the static Pod manifests on the node it owns.

The modules map onto the pieces of that job:

:mod:static_sets.models The StaticSet custom resource and its policies and status. :mod:static_sets.placements The StaticPodPlacement record: the durable fact "this node hosts this revision of this StaticSet". :mod:static_sets.workload The supported subset of PodTemplateSpec: what can be compiled, and what is rejected rather than silently dropped. :mod:static_sets.translation The compiler, including its Secret-handling rules. :mod:static_sets.revision Deterministic revision identity. :mod:static_sets.probe The scheduling probe, which is how the Kubernetes scheduler is asked for a placement. :mod:static_sets.controller The pure reconcile planner and status builder. :mod:static_sets.manager The on-node runtime, including the offline behaviour and the rollout order. :mod:static_sets.install Durable, ownership-checked installation of a revision on a node. :mod:static_sets.paths Path validation and durable write primitives.

def __post_init__(self) -> None:
    """Refuse a node configuration that would write into kubelet's path.

    Raises:
        DefinitionError: If either path is not absolute, or they overlap.
    """
    for field_name in ("static_pod_path", "bundle_dir"):
        value: str = getattr(self, field_name)
        if not _is_absolute(value):
            raise DefinitionError(
                f"the manager's {field_name} must be an absolute path, got {value!r}"
            )
    if _overlaps(self.static_pod_path, self.bundle_dir):
        raise DefinitionError(
            f"the manager's staticPodPath ({self.static_pod_path!r}) and bundleDir "
            f"({self.bundle_dir!r}) must be disjoint: kubelet watches the static Pod "
            "path, so temporary and revision files must not live beneath it"
        )

def for_placement(
    cls,
    *,
    namespace: str,
    static_set: str,
    uid: str,
    node: str,
    generation: int,
    instance: str,
    static_pod_path: str,
    bundle_dir: str,
) -> Assignment:
    """Build an assignment, deriving the placement identity.

    Args:
        namespace: The StaticSet's namespace.
        static_set: The StaticSet's name.
        uid: The StaticSet's UID.
        node: The node this manager owns.
        generation: The placement's generation.
        instance: The manager Pod's name.
        static_pod_path: kubelet's static Pod path.
        bundle_dir: The persistent bundle directory.

    Returns:
        The assignment.
    """
    return cls(
        namespace=namespace,
        static_set=static_set,
        uid=uid,
        node=node,
        identity=placement_identity(uid, node),
        generation=generation,
        instance=instance,
        static_pod_path=static_pod_path,
        bundle_dir=bundle_dir,
    )

def manifest_path_for(self, pod_name: str) -> str:
    """Return the manifest path kubelet reads for one static Pod name.

    The name carries the revision, so the previous revision's file and the new
    one's are different paths — which is what a ``Surge`` rollout needs.

    Args:
        pod_name: The static Pod's name.

    Returns:
        The absolute manifest path.
    """
    return f"{self.static_pod_path.rstrip('/')}/{manifest_filename(pod_name)}"

def revision_dir(self, revision: str) -> str:
    """Return the directory that holds one revision's content.

    Args:
        revision: The revision token.

    Returns:
        The absolute revision directory.

    Raises:
        InstallationError: If the token is not a well-formed revision, which
            would otherwise let a caller inject a path.
    """
    if not is_revision(revision):
        raise InstallationError(f"{revision!r} is not a well-formed revision token")
    return f"{self.revisions_dir}/{revision}"

def payload(self) -> dict[str, str]:
    """Return the status payload a manager publishes.

    Returns:
        The payload, with every value a string because the transport may be a
        merge patch over a CRD status.
    """
    return {
        "revision": self.revision or "",
        "staticPodName": self.static_pod_name or "",
        "phase": self.phase.value,
        "acknowledged": "true" if self.acknowledged else "false",
        "offline": "true" if self.offline else "false",
        "warnings": " | ".join(self.warnings),
        "message": self.message or "",
    }

(Placement, default: <dynamic> ) –

Where the operator may schedule installers.

These settings steer the scheduler, which places installer Pods. They are not copied onto the emitted static workload, because kubelet never schedules a static Pod: it starts the file it finds on the node whose kubelet finds it.

The field types are the official Kubernetes ones, so the CRD documents the scheduler API faithfully; the validator below refuses the parts this operator does not act on, rather than accepting them and quietly ignoring them.

claim_placement(
    layout: PlacementLayout,
    *,
    static_set: str,
    static_set_uid: str,
    namespace: str,
    node: str,
    generation: int,
    owner: str,
    now: str
) -> OwnershipRecord

Take ownership of a placement's local state, handed over or fresh.

Handover is generation-aware: a successor may adopt a placement recorded for an older or equal generation, which is what lets an installer replace one that disappeared on the same node. A record from a newer generation is authoritative and is never overwritten, so a resurrected stale Pod cannot reclaim a placement that has already moved on.

Parameters:

Raises:

    If the existing record belongs to another StaticSet or to a newer generation.

Source code in src/static_sets/install.py 
def claim_placement(
    layout: PlacementLayout,
    *,
    static_set: str,
    static_set_uid: str,
    namespace: str,
    node: str,
    generation: int,
    owner: str,
    now: str,
) -> OwnershipRecord:
    """Take ownership of a placement's local state, handed over or fresh.

    Handover is generation-aware: a successor may adopt a placement recorded for an
    older or equal generation, which is what lets an installer replace one that
    disappeared on the same node. A record from a *newer* generation is authoritative
    and is never overwritten, so a resurrected stale Pod cannot reclaim a placement
    that has already moved on.

    Args:
        layout: The placement's layout.
        static_set: The owning StaticSet's name.
        static_set_uid: The owning StaticSet's UID.
        namespace: The StaticSet's namespace.
        node: The node name.
        generation: The generation the current reconcile is for.
        owner: The calling installer's instance identity.
        now: The current time, RFC 3339.

    Returns:
        The record now in force.

    Raises:
        OwnershipError: If the existing record belongs to another StaticSet or to a
            newer generation.
    """
    existing = read_record(layout)
    if existing is not None:
        if existing.static_set_uid != static_set_uid:
            raise OwnershipError(
                f"placement {layout.identity} belongs to StaticSet uid "
                f"{existing.static_set_uid}, not to {static_set_uid}"
            )
        if existing.generation > generation:
            raise OwnershipError(
                f"placement {layout.identity} was taken over at generation "
                f"{existing.generation}, which is newer than {generation}"
            )
    record = OwnershipRecord(
        placement=layout.identity,
        pod_name=layout.pod_name,
        static_set=static_set,
        static_set_uid=static_set_uid,
        namespace=namespace,
        node=node,
        generation=generation,
        revision=existing.revision if existing is not None else None,
        retiring=existing.retiring if existing is not None else None,
        history=list(existing.history) if existing is not None else [],
        state="Installing",
        owner=owner,
        updated_at=now,
    )
    _write_record(layout, record)
    return record

def cleanup(
    assignment: Assignment,
    *,
    api: PlacementApi,
    now: str,
    reason: str,
    remove_configuration: bool,
) -> PlacementReport:
    """Remove the static Pod of a placement that is no longer wanted.

    Args:
        assignment: The placement and the manager's node configuration.
        api: The Kubernetes API slice it may use.
        now: The current time, RFC 3339.
        reason: Why the placement is being removed, as the controller recorded it.
        remove_configuration: Whether materialized configuration may be deleted once
            the workload is confirmed stopped.

    Returns:
        The report to publish.

    Raises:
        ApiUnavailableError: If the API cannot be reached, in which case nothing is
            removed.
        StaticSetsError: If the local record disagrees with the placement about
            ownership, which means the placement has been taken over.
    """
    record = read_record(assignment.layout(_cleanup_pod_name(assignment)))
    layout = assignment.layout(
        record.pod_name if record is not None else _cleanup_pod_name(assignment)
    )
    intent = CleanupIntent(
        placement=assignment.identity,
        pod_name=record.pod_name if record is not None else _cleanup_pod_name(assignment),
        static_set=assignment.static_set,
        static_set_uid=assignment.uid,
        namespace=assignment.namespace,
        node=assignment.node,
        generation=assignment.generation,
        reason=reason,
        remove_configuration=remove_configuration,
        requested_at=now,
    )
    # Persisted before anything is touched, so a crash between learning of the
    # removal and finishing it leaves the intent discoverable.
    write_intent(layout, intent)
    terminated = _terminated(api, assignment, _installed_revisions(record))
    outcome = remove_workload(layout, intent=intent, terminated=terminated)
    return PlacementReport(
        revision=None,
        static_pod_name=None,
        phase=PlacementPhase.CLEANED if outcome.acknowledged else PlacementPhase.CLEANING,
        acknowledged=outcome.acknowledged,
        message=outcome.message,
    )
